onepagr's built-in templates are checked with software checkers: PAC, run by
hand on each rendered template, veraPDF (PDF/UA-1 profile) run from the
command line, and Typst's own `--pdf-standard ua-1` compile, plus computed
WCAG contrast ratios. Software checkers can only decide part of what
accessibility requires. This vignette explains where that line falls and
gives a short checklist for the part that needs a person.

It describes what was checked. It is not a statement of legal compliance
with the ADA, Section 508, or any other law or regulation.

## What software checkers can and cannot decide

The PDF Association's [Matterhorn
Protocol](https://pdfa.org/resource/the-matterhorn-protocol/) (version
1.1) is the common testing model for PDF/UA-1. It breaks the standard into
31 checkpoints and 136 failure conditions. Of those, 87 can be decided by
software alone, 47 usually need human judgment, and 2 have no specific test.
Each condition is marked `M` (machine) or `H` (human) in the protocol.

So when veraPDF and PAC report no failures, that covers the machine-testable
conditions. It says nothing about whether alt text is meaningful, whether
the reading order makes sense, or whether a bold label should have been a
heading. PAC's AI-assisted tab tries to catch some of these, but it is a
heuristic advisory, not a conformance check.

The built-in templates are built so that the human-judgment items below come
out right on the sample content. Your own content changes some of them, and
a custom theme or template changes others, so the checklist applies to what
you actually produce.

## Checklist for the human-judgment conditions

Condition numbers are the Matterhorn Protocol's, so you can look up the
exact wording.

**Structure and reading order**

- *Reading order* (09-001). Open the PDF in PAC and view the logical
  structure and the screen reader preview. Confirm the order matches how a
  sighted reader would read both pages, including callout boxes and any
  side-by-side layouts.
- *Tags fit their content* (01-001, 01-002, 01-006, 09-002, 09-003). Look for
  real content left as an artifact, decoration tagged as content, and
  elements whose tag does not match what is inside them.
- *Headings* (14-001, 14-004, 14-005). Every visually bold section label
  should be a real heading, and levels should not skip. A label written as
  styled text looks like a heading but is tagged as a paragraph, and the
  PDF/UA and WCAG checks pass it anyway.

**Graphics and meaning**

- *Alt text* (13-001 to 13-008). Every chart, map, and logo that carries
  meaning needs alt text that conveys what a sighted reader gets from it,
  not "chart" or a file name. Purely decorative images should be artifacts.
- *Color alone* (04-001). If severity, category, or status is shown only by
  color, such as red versus green or a bivariate map, a text or shape cue
  must carry the same meaning. Contrast ratios cover legibility, not this.

**Tables and lists**

- *Tables* (15-001 to 15-005). Content with real rows and columns should be
  structured as a table, and content that is not tabular should not be. The
  built-in bar-row groups use a grid, not a table, and PAC's AI-assisted
  tab notes this. Decide whether that is acceptable for your readers.
- *Lists* (16-001 to 16-003). Anything that is a list should be tagged as
  one.

**Page furniture and notes**

- *Headers and footers* (18-001, 18-002). Repeating page furniture should be
  marked as artifacts. On the fixed-page templates (`cohort_summary`,
  `trend_snapshot`, `county_choropleth`) the footer also carries real
  content, such as the organization name and contact details, so it is
  tagged as content on purpose. The two alert templates
  (`overdose_spike_alert`, `syndromic_alert`) cannot do this: their page
  count depends on the content, Typst leaves everything in a page footer
  out of the tag tree, and a walk of their PDFs shows one tagged figure
  (the header logo) and no links. A screen reader does not reach their footer
  logos, organization name, contact URL or email. Repeat contact details
  in body text on those templates, for example in `footnote_sources`.
- *Notes* (19-001, 19-002). Footnote-like text should be tagged as a note.
  Typst 0.15.1 cannot produce a note tag, so the footer's sources line is a
  paragraph. This is a toolchain gap, not something a template can fix.

**Document-level**

- *Title* (06-004). The `dc:title` should identify the document, not just
  exist. The templates take it from your `doc_title`.
- *Language* (11-007). Confirm the declared language is correct, and that
  passages in another language are marked.
- *Fonts* (31-010). If a theme loads fonts through `font_dir`, confirm the
  font license allows embedding. Software can read the embedding flag, but
  that may not match the actual license.

A few conditions in the protocol do not apply to these templates at all, for
example math, forms, media, scripts, and article threads.

## Listening to the result

The most informative single test is to run a screen reader over a rendered
PDF. NVDA is free on Windows and reads PDFs in Adobe Reader or Foxit.
VoiceOver does the same on macOS. It exposes reading order, missing labels,
and odd announcements in a way no checker does. Doing it once per template
with one theme is a reasonable bar.

Two quick supporting checks:

- Copy text out of the PDF and paste it somewhere. Scrambled order here is a
  cheap warning that the reading order is wrong.
- Use the keyboard alone to reach every link.

## Customizing

If you write your own theme or template, re-run PAC and veraPDF on the
result, and walk the checklist above again. A color or layout choice that
passes in one template is not automatically safe in another. See
`vignette("theming")` for the contrast rules the built-in themes follow.

## Source

The condition numbers and the 87, 47, and 2 split come from the PDF
Association's Matterhorn Protocol 1.1 (2021), licensed CC-BY-4.0. The
[landing page](https://pdfa.org/resource/the-matterhorn-protocol/) has the
description and version history, and the
[PDF itself](https://pdfa.org/download-area/publications/Matterhorn-Protocol-1-1.pdf)
is a direct download.
